title: Is dividing by zero point four the same as dividing by four?
description: One hundred and twenty eight is divided by four and by zero point four, and both answers are compared with one hundred and twenty eight. Keeko doubts that dividing always gives a smaller number.
teaching_notes: One idea: a divisor smaller than one fits into the number more times than the number itself. Watch for children who think dividing always makes a number smaller.

video_script.why: The child can divide by a counting number and now meets a decimal divisor, where multiplying both numbers by ten turns the divisor into a counting number.
video_script.substitution: the book's own comparison of one hundred and twenty eight divided by four and by zero point four
video_script.anchor: One hundred and twenty eight divided by four, and by zero point four
video_script.wrong_answer: dividing always gives a smaller number
video_script.wrong_move: A common slip thinks dividing always gives a smaller number, so one hundred and twenty eight divided by zero point four must be less than one hundred and twenty eight. But zero point four is less than one, so more pieces fit than the number itself.
video_script.payoff_line: The first answer is smaller and the second answer is bigger.

final_answer.value: 32 is smaller than 128; 320 is bigger than 128
final_answer.spoken: thirty two is smaller than one hundred and twenty eight, and three hundred and twenty is bigger than one hundred and twenty eight

maths_rules: 1280 ÷ 4: 12 hundreds ÷ 4 = 3 hundreds, 8 tens ÷ 4 = 2 tens, 0 ones, so 320
320 > 128, since 0.4 is less than 1 and 2.5 pieces of 0.4 fit in each 1, and 2.5 × 128 = 320
the slip: dividing always gives a smaller number
video_script.design: One idea: a divisor less than one fits into the number more times than the number itself, so the quotient is bigger. Assumes division by a counting number. Wrong idea: dividing always makes a number smaller. The two divisions stay all video; the quotient three hundred and twenty appears only on the answer beat.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Dividing asks how many pieces of the divisor fit into the number.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>A big piece fits fewer times.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>A small piece, shorter than one, fits more times. In one whole, two and a half pieces of zero point four fit.
<bookmark mark='m1'/>Given, one hundred and twenty eight divided by four.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>And one hundred and twenty eight divided by zero point four.

<bookmark mark='m2'/>Four times thirty two is one hundred and twenty eight, so the quotient is thirty two.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Thirty two is smaller than one hundred and twenty eight.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, divide by zero point four. Multiply both numbers by ten, so that the divisor is a counting number.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>One hundred and twenty eight times ten is one thousand two hundred and eighty.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Zero point four times ten is four.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, divide one thousand two hundred and eighty by four. Twelve hundreds shared by four give three hundreds.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Eight tens shared by four give two tens.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Zero ones shared by four give zero ones.

<bookmark mark='m2'/>Divided by four, we get thirty two, which is smaller than one hundred and twenty eight.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Divided by zero point four, we get three hundred and twenty, which is bigger.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Keeko thinks dividing always gives a smaller number.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>But zero point four is less than one, so its pieces are small. Two and a half of them fit in each whole.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>In one hundred and twenty eight wholes, many more pieces fit, and the answer grows.
